theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You are given a work order for a conduit wiring job. What should you do first?
options: Read the work order and drawings so you know what the job needs
Start fixing conduit at the panel and work outward from there
Buy the materials you think you need, then look at the drawings
Ask the customer to point out where each outlet should be fitted

questions.stem: What does the job specification (the "spec") tell an electrician?
options: The pay rate for each worker and how often they are paid
The names and phone numbers of the other trades on site
The type and quality of materials and how the work is done
The date the job must be finished, and nothing else about it

questions.stem: A layout drawing has a scale of 1:50. A conduit run measures 80 mm on the drawing. How long is the real run?
options: 4 m
8 m

questions.stem: Where on a drawing do you find out what each symbol means?
options: In the title block, beside the drawing number
In the revision box in the bottom corner
In the scale bar along the bottom edge
In the legend, which is also called the key

questions.stem: Why must you check the revision letter on a drawing before you start work?
options: To find out who drew it and on what date it was printed
To make sure you are working from the latest version
To work out which scale was used for the floor plan
To find out how many sheets are in the full drawing set

questions.stem: Before you mark out a conduit route in an existing building, what must you look for along the route?
options: Hidden pipes, cables and other services in walls and floors
The colour the walls will be painted when the job is done
The make and model of the switches the owner already has
Places where the owner may want extra outlets some day

questions.stem: Why are draw-in (pull) boxes planned along a long conduit route with several bends?
options: So the conduit can be fixed to the wall without saddles
So water that gets in can drain out of the conduit
So fewer cables are needed to supply the same outlets
So cables can be pulled in without strain or damage

questions.stem: What is a risk assessment?
options: A list of the tools and materials you will need for the job
A form the customer signs to say the work has been finished
A check of what could cause harm and how to control it
A test of the wiring that is done after the job is complete

questions.stem: You find old cement sheeting that may contain asbestos where you need to drill. What should you do?
options: Wet it with water and drill through it slowly and carefully
Wear a dust mask and drill quickly to keep the dust down
Stop, leave it alone and report it to your supervisor
Break it out with a hammer so that it is out of the way

questions.stem: Which is the correct order for the safe isolation of a circuit?
options: Switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a tester
Prove dead with a tester, then switch off and lock off
Switch off, start the work, then lock off when there is time
Lock off and tag, then switch off once the work has begun

questions.stem: Why do you check the voltage tester on a known live source or proving unit both before and after you test the circuit?
options: To charge the tester's battery so that it reads correctly
To prove the tester worked when it showed no voltage
To show the customer that the supply is now switched back on
To warm up the tester so that it gives a steady reading

questions.stem: Why do you fit your own padlock when you lock off an isolator?
options: So that the isolator looks neat when the job is finished
So that the customer knows the job has been paid for
So that the power company can read the meter later
So that nobody else can switch it on while you work

questions.stem: What should a danger tag on a locked-off isolator show?
options: Not to switch on, who is working, and the date
The size of cable in the circuit that is being worked on
The price of the job and when the customer will pay
The name of the maker of the isolator and its rating

questions.stem: Which PPE should you wear when drilling holes in a concrete block wall for conduit fixings?
options: Gloves only, because the drill bit gets very hot
A welding helmet with a dark shade and a leather apron
Sunglasses and a cap to keep the dust off your face
Safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection

questions.stem: Before you climb a stepladder to mark out a ceiling run, what should you check?
options: That the ladder has been painted so it does not rust
That the feet, steps and spreaders are sound and locked
That the ladder is tall enough to stand on the very top
That it is a metal ladder, because metal is the strongest

questions.stem: Why should an electrician use a fibreglass or wooden ladder rather than an aluminium one?
options: Aluminium ladders are too heavy to carry around the site
Aluminium ladders cannot be opened out as a stepladder
Fibreglass and wood do not conduct electricity like metal
Fibreglass and wooden ladders never need to be inspected

questions.stem: Which type of conduit is best for a run in a damp, salty place, such as a building near the sea?
options: Plain steel conduit with no protective coating
Thin-wall steel tubing with set-screw fittings
Flexible metal conduit along the whole run
Rigid PVC conduit with solvent-cement joints

questions.stem: What is flexible conduit mainly used for?
options: Long straight runs along the walls and the ceilings
Short final runs to equipment that moves or vibrates
Runs that are buried directly in the ground outside
The main supply run from the meter to the panel board

questions.stem: What is a conduit coupling used for?
options: To join two lengths of conduit end to end
To fix the conduit to the wall or ceiling
To change the direction of the run by 90°
To seal the open end of a conduit run

questions.stem: What is a saddle clip (strap) used for in a conduit installation?
options: To join a length of conduit to a box
To make a 90° bend in a conduit run
To hold the conduit firmly to the surface
To protect cable where it leaves the conduit

questions.stem: Why should all the conduit, fittings and boxes on one run be from the same system and size?
options: So that the job looks the same colour everywhere
So that the drawings can be made at a smaller scale
So that joints fit properly and stay strong and sealed
So that fewer saddles are needed to hold the run up

questions.stem: How is the size of cable for a new circuit chosen?
options: Use the largest cable on the van, just to be safe
Use the same size of cable as on the last job you did
Choose the size by the colour of the insulation
Follow the drawing and the code for the load and length

questions.stem: Before you use cable and accessories on a job, what should you check them for?
options: The right type and rating, and no damage
The shop's name printed on each item
That every item is the cheapest one available
That they are the same colour as the wall

questions.stem: Which tool is used to check that a conduit run is truly horizontal?
options: A plumb bob
A spirit level
A try square
A tape measure

questions.stem: Which tool is used to mark a long straight line on a wall for a conduit run?
options: A centre punch
A chalk line
A scriber
A pipe wrench

questions.stem: Before using a portable electric drill, what should you check?
options: That the chuck key is taped onto the power cable
That the drill is the heaviest one in the store
That the cable, plug and casing are not damaged
That someone else has used the drill earlier today

questions.stem: What should you do with a tool that you find is damaged?
options: Label it, take it out of use and report it
Use it carefully until the job is finished
Fix it yourself with tape and carry on with it
Put it back in the store for someone else

questions.stem: A conduit run is 14 m long. Conduit comes in 3 m lengths. What is the least number of lengths you need?
Why should a materials list (take-off) be made before the job starts?
options: So that the drawings do not need to be read on site
So that the job can start before the drawings arrive
So that the job needs no supervisor to check it
So the right items are on site when they are needed

questions.stem: The drawing says to fix saddles every 1 m along a 9 m straight run, with one at each end. How many saddles are needed?
What should you use to find the positions of switches, outlets and boxes on site?
options: The positions the last electrician used in another house
Your own idea of where they will look best on the wall
The heights and positions shown on the drawing
The places where the wall is easiest to drill into

questions.stem: Why do you measure box positions from a fixed datum line, such as the finished floor level?
options: So that the measuring tape does not wear out quickly
So that every box is set at the same, correct height
So that the boxes can be fixed without any screws
So that the floor tiles can be laid after the wiring

questions.stem: What is the main reason for marking out the whole route before you fix any conduit?
options: To find clashes and problems before materials are cut
To use up spare chalk and marker pens on the site
To show the customer how long the job will take
To avoid having to read the drawing again later

questions.stem: A plumber plans to run water pipes along the same wall as your conduit. What should you do?
options: Fix your conduit first so the plumber must go around it
Agree the routes with the plumber and your supervisor
Run your conduit directly on top of the water pipes
Leave the job until the plumber has finished all the work

questions.stem: The drawing shows an outlet in a place where a door now opens. What should you do?
options: Fit the outlet behind the door as the drawing shows
Leave the outlet out and say nothing to anybody
Move it to any place you like and carry on working
Report it and ask your supervisor where it should go

questions.stem: How should lengths of conduit be stored on site?
options: Standing upright against a wall where people walk
In a loose pile in the doorway so they are close by
Flat on racks or supports, off the ground and tidy
Out in the sun on bare ground until they are used

questions.stem: Why must the work area be kept clear of off-cuts and cable scraps?
options: So that the scraps can be sold at the end of the job
So that the customer cannot see how much was wasted
So that nobody trips or slips while moving around
So that the materials list looks right at the end

questions.stem: Why should you record any change you make to the planned conduit route?
options: So that you can charge the customer extra for each change
So that the supervisor knows who to blame later on
So that the job can be finished without any testing
So the as-built drawings show where cables really run

questions.stem: What does a yellow triangle sign with a black lightning flash mean?
options: Fire exit this way
Danger of electric shock
Wear eye protection
First-aid kit inside

questions.stem: Why should you look for overhead power lines before carrying long lengths of conduit or a ladder outside?
options: Conduit or a ladder touching a line can cause a fatal shock
Power lines make conduit change colour in the hot sun
The power company charges for any work done near lines
Long conduit lengths will bend if they touch a wire

questions.stem: Why should you wear safety boots on a building site?
options: To keep your feet cool in the hot weather on site
To make it easier to climb ladders quickly
To stop dust getting onto the drawings on site
To protect your feet from falling items and nails

questions.stem: Before you switch off a supply in a building that people are using, what should you do?
options: Tell the people affected and agree a time with them
Switch off quickly so that nobody has time to complain
Switch off the main supply to the whole street
Wait until night so that nobody will notice it

questions.stem: When proving a 110 V single-phase circuit dead, between which conductors should you test?
options: Line to neutral only, once at the panel
Line to earth only, once at the outlet
Line to neutral, line to earth and neutral to earth
Neutral to earth only, at the outlet furthest away

questions.stem: At the end of the preparation stage, what should you tell your supervisor?
options: Only the time that you arrived on site this morning
That all is ready, and any problems you found
Nothing at all, unless the customer has complained
How much you think the next job ought to cost

questions.stem: What should you do with off-cuts of PVC conduit and empty solvent cement tins?
options: Burn them on site at the end of the day
Bury them in the yard behind the building
Put them in the right waste bins for disposal
Leave them in the ceiling space out of sight

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would safely isolate an existing circuit before you prepare to extend it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the right circuit from the board schedule and the drawing, and I tell the people in the building that the power will be off. I switch off the circuit breaker or isolator for that circuit. I lock it off with my own padlock and keep the key in my pocket, and I fit a danger tag with my name, the date and 'Do not switch on'. Next I check my approved voltage tester on a known live source or a proving unit to show that it works. Then I test at the point of work between line and neutral, line and earth, and neutral and earth. When it shows dead, I check the tester again on the proving unit, to make sure it did not fail during the test. Only then do I start work. I never work on a live circuit.
markingPoints: Identifies the right circuit and tells the people affected
Switches off, then locks off with own lock and keeps the key
Fits a danger tag with name, date and 'do not switch on'
Proves the tester before and after, and tests between all conductors at the point of work
Starts work only when proved dead; never works live

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan a conduit route from a distribution board to a switch, a light and two outlets, using the drawing and a visit to the site.
essays.modelAnswer: I start by reading the drawing, the legend and the specification, so I know where each point goes, what conduit and cable to use and what heights to work to. Then I walk the route on site with the drawing. I look for things in the way, such as beams, windows, pipes and air-conditioning units, and I check for hidden cables and pipes before any drilling. I plan a neat route that runs straight, level and parallel to the walls and ceiling, with as few bends as possible. I plan where boxes, bends and draw-in points go, so that the cables can be pulled in easily later. I agree any change with my supervisor and mark it on the drawing. Last, I make a materials list for the route.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing, legend and specification first
Walks the route and looks for obstacles and hidden services
Plans straight, level runs parallel to the building lines with few bends
Places boxes and draw-in points so cables can be pulled in
Agrees changes with the supervisor and records them

essays.stem: Name four hazards you might find when preparing for a conduit installation in a building that people are using, and say how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Live circuits: I find out which circuits are near the work, and I isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead any circuit I will work on. Working at height: I use a sound fibreglass stepladder or a platform, set up on firm, level ground, and I do not stand on the top step. Dust and noise from drilling block: I wear safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection, and I keep other people away. Trips from tools, leads and off-cuts: I keep the area tidy, put up signs or barriers, and run leads where people do not walk. Hidden pipes and cables: I check the drawings and use a detector before drilling. I write these in a risk assessment and tell my supervisor.
markingPoints: Live circuits controlled by safe isolation (switch off, lock, tag, prove dead)
Work at height controlled by a sound non-conducting ladder set up correctly
Dust and noise controlled with PPE and keeping others away
Trips and the public controlled by tidiness, signs or barriers
Hidden services found by checking drawings and using a detector

essays.stem: Compare PVC conduit and steel conduit. Say where you would use each one, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: PVC conduit is light, cheap, easy to cut and easy to join with solvent cement, and it does not rust. It suits most homes in Jamaica, runs cast in concrete or block, damp places and buildings near the sea. It does not conduct, so a separate earth conductor is always drawn in. It softens if it gets too hot, and it grows and shrinks with the temperature, so long runs in the sun need expansion couplings. Steel conduit is strong and protects cables well from knocks, so it is used in workshops, factories and places where it could be hit. It can be part of the earth path where the code allows, if every joint is tight. It is heavier, harder to cut and bend, and it can rust near the sea unless it is galvanised and kept painted.
markingPoints: PVC: light, easy to cut and join, does not rust
PVC uses: homes, damp or salty places, cast in concrete or block
PVC needs a separate earth conductor and allows for heat and expansion
Steel: strong, protects against knocks; used in workshops and factories
Steel: heavier, harder to work, can rust unless protected

essays.stem: Describe the checks you would make on hand tools, power tools and ladders before you use them on site.
essays.modelAnswer: For hand tools, I check that the handles are tight and not cracked, that blades and cutting edges are sharp, and that insulated tools have no cuts or splits in the insulation. For power tools, I check the cable, plug and casing for damage, that the tool has an in-date inspection label, that the guard and switch work, and that the right bit or blade is fitted tightly. For battery tools, I check the battery and charger. For ladders, I check that the stiles, rungs or steps are not cracked or bent, that the feet are in place and that the spreaders lock. I use fibreglass or wooden ladders for electrical work. Any damaged item is labelled, taken out of use and reported, and never used.
markingPoints: Hand tools: handles, edges and insulation checked
Power tools: cable, plug, casing, guard, switch and inspection label checked
Ladders: stiles, rungs or steps, feet and spreaders checked
Uses a fibreglass or wooden ladder for electrical work
Damaged items labelled, taken out of use and reported

essays.stem: Explain how you would work out a materials list (take-off) for a conduit job from the drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the drawing and specification to find the type and size of conduit, cable and accessories. Using the legend, I count each item shown, such as boxes, switches, outlets and light points. I measure each conduit run with a scale rule and use the scale to change it to a real length, and I add the drops down the walls to each box. I add up the runs, divide by the length of one piece of conduit and round up, with a little extra for waste. I count the bends, couplings, saddles, screws and plugs for each run. For cable, I add the run lengths for each conductor and allow extra for the connections. I write the list as a table with item, size and quantity, and my supervisor checks it.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing, legend and specification
Counts accessories and boxes from the drawing
Measures runs with a scale rule and converts to real lengths, including drops
Adds fittings, saddles and fixings, rounds up and allows for waste
Writes a clear list and has it checked

essays.stem: Describe how you would mark out the route and box positions for a surface conduit run on a block wall.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the drawing for the position and height of each box. I measure up from the finished floor level, or from a datum line, and mark the centre of each box. I use a spirit level or a laser level to mark a level line for the horizontal run, and a plumb bob or level for each vertical drop. I snap a chalk line between the marks to show the run clearly. Along the line I mark where each bend, box and saddle will go. I check the marks against the drawing again, and I use a detector to look for hidden pipes or cables at each fixing point. Finally I ask my supervisor to check the marking before any drilling or fixing is done.
markingPoints: Takes positions and heights from the drawing
Measures from finished floor level or a datum
Marks level and plumb lines with the right tools, then a chalk line
Marks bends, boxes and saddle positions; checks for hidden services
Has the marking checked before fixing

essays.stem: Why is it important to talk with your supervisor, the customer and other trades before you start a conduit job? Give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: Talking first saves time and stops mistakes. My supervisor can confirm that I have the latest drawing, explain the job and agree any change to the route. The customer needs to know when the power will be off and where we will work, and may need to move furniture. The customer may also tell me about hidden pipes, or about changes they want. Other trades, such as plumbers, masons and air-conditioning fitters, may be using the same walls and ceilings. If we agree the routes and the order of work, our conduit will not clash with their pipes or ducts, and nothing will need to be taken out later. Good communication also keeps everyone safe, for example when a circuit is isolated.
markingPoints: Supervisor: latest drawing, job details, agreed changes
Customer: power-off times, access, hidden services or changes
Other trades: avoids clashes and agrees the order of work
Keeps people safe, for example during isolation
Saves time, cost and rework

essays.stem: Explain how materials and tools should be stored, and the work area kept, during a conduit job, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Conduit is stored flat on racks or supports, off the ground and out of the sun, so it does not bend, get dirty or soften. Fittings, boxes and screws are kept in labelled boxes so that they are easy to find. Cable drums are stood on a stand or wedged so that they cannot roll. Solvent cement is kept closed, away from heat and flames. Tools are kept in a tool box or locked store and cleaned after use, and power tools are unplugged when they are not being used. The work area is swept often, and off-cuts go straight into bins. This stops trips and falls, protects materials from damage and theft, and makes the job quicker.
markingPoints: Conduit stored flat, supported, off the ground and out of the sun
Small fittings kept sorted and labelled; cable drums secured
Solvent cement and other flammables closed and away from heat
Tools stored safely, cleaned, and unplugged when not in use
Area swept and off-cuts binned to prevent trips, damage and loss

essays.stem: What should you report and record at the end of preparing for a conduit job, and why?
essays.modelAnswer: I tell my supervisor that the route is marked out, that the materials and tools are on site and checked, and that the area is safe for work to start. I report any problem, such as a clash with a pipe, a mistake on the drawing, missing or damaged materials, or a hazard such as possible asbestos. I write any change to the route on the drawing so that the as-built drawings will be correct. I record which circuits are isolated and locked off, and who holds the keys. I fill in the job sheet or daily report with the time spent and the materials used. This keeps everyone informed and safe, and it helps with costing and with future work on the building.
markingPoints: Reports that the route, materials and tools are ready
Reports problems and hazards found
Marks route changes on the drawing for as-built records
Records isolated circuits and who holds the keys
Completes the job sheet or daily report

practical1.title: Survey, plan and mark out a conduit route on a training bay
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a simple drawing of a training bay (or a room at the Centre) that shows a distribution board, one switch, one light and two outlets. As a group, read the drawing and the legend, walk the route, and complete a short risk assessment. Then mark out the full conduit route on the wall: the box positions and heights from the datum, level and plumb lines, bends, draw-in boxes and saddle positions. Last, write a materials list (take-off) for the job. Share the work so that every member marks out at least one run or box position while the assessor watches, and every member helps with the risk assessment and the materials list. Nothing is connected to a supply. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the marking out is finished and the area is tidy.
materials: Drawing of the training bay or room, with legend and scale (from the assessor)
Tape measure, spirit level (or laser level), plumb bob and chalk line
Scale rule, pencils and a marker
Risk assessment form and materials list form
photos: The group reading the drawing and legend together
The datum line and box positions marked, with the tape measure in view
A level line being checked with the spirit level
The whole route marked out, with bends, boxes and saddle positions
The work area left clean and tidy
checklist: Read the drawing, legend and scale correctly and found each point on site
Took part in the risk assessment and named real hazards with sensible controls
Checked for hidden cables and pipes before marking fixing points
Measured box heights from the datum or finished floor level as the drawing shows
Marked straight, level and plumb lines with the right tools
Planned bends and draw-in boxes so cables can be pulled in easily
Worked out quantities correctly on the materials list, rounding lengths up
Reported any problem with the drawing or route to the assessor
safety: Use a sound stepladder set up on firm, level ground; never stand on the top step
Treat all existing wiring as live; do not open any board or accessory
Keep walkways clear of tools, leads and materials
Wear safety boots; wear safety glasses if any drilling is allowed
Follow the maker's instructions for every tool and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Safe isolation drill, and selecting and checking materials and tools for a conduit job
practical2.brief: Part A: On the Centre's safe isolation training board, which is not connected to any supply, each member in turn carries out the full safe isolation steps while the assessor watches: identify the circuit, switch off, lock off with their own lock, fit a filled-in danger tag, prove the voltage tester on the proving unit, test between all conductors at the point of work, prove the tester again, and then remove the lock and tag correctly when told. Part B: Using the materials list from the assessor, the group collects the conduit, fittings, boxes, saddles, fixings and cable from the store. Check each item for the right type, size and condition, and set aside and label any damaged item. Then lay out and check the tools for the job. Every member checks at least one group of items. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Safe isolation training board (not connected to any supply)
Approved two-pole voltage tester and a proving unit
Padlocks, lock-off devices and danger tags (one set for each member)
Conduit, couplings, bends, boxes, saddles, screws, wall plugs and cable from the store
Hand tools and power tools for a conduit job
Labels and a marker for damaged items
photos: Each member's lock and danger tag fitted on the isolator
The voltage tester being proved on the proving unit
The tester probes on the test points of the board
Materials laid out and ticked off against the list
Any damaged item labelled and set aside
The store and work area left tidy
checklist: Identified the correct circuit before switching off
Locked off with own lock, kept the key, and fitted a filled-in danger tag
Proved the tester on the proving unit before and after testing
Tested between line and neutral, line and earth, and neutral and earth
Did not touch any conductor before the circuit was proved dead
Checked materials for the right type, size and condition against the list
Checked tools (leads, plugs, handles, insulation) and labelled any faulty item
Removed the lock and tag only when told the work was finished
safety: The training board must not be connected to any supply during this task
Never work live; if in doubt, stop and ask the assessor
Carry long lengths of conduit with a partner and watch for people and light fittings
Lift with your legs, not your back, and get help with heavy cable drums
Follow the tester maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
